newsitem.title: USA: Ford sees Japanese gaining in U.S. car market.
newsitem.headline: Ford sees Japanese gaining in U.S. car market.

text.p: Japanese automakers are expected to gain a bigger share of the U.S. car market in January because the weak yen has allowed them to sell at more aggressive prices, Ford Motor Co's Chief Financial Officer John Devine said on Wednesday.
Devine said that the yen's fall is starting to put significant pressure on Detroit's Big Three U.S. automakers.

"It's going to impact us. I can already see it happening in January," Devine told reporters at a news briefing. "If you watch the Japanese share in January, I think you're going to see big up (increases) in the car business," he said.
Automakers are expected to report January U.S. car and light truck sales February 3-5.
Devine said Japanese previously used the weakness of the yen to improve their profit margins, but are now using it as a weapon to increase market share.

At the current exchange rate of about 121.8 yen to the dollar, he said Japanese automakers can supplement constrained U.S. production by importing more cars from Japan without much of a financial penalty.
"This is not a whine," Devine said. "Believe me, we're working our brains out to get our costs down. In the stroke of a couple months of exchange rate movements, that's wiped out."

Earlier Wednesday, the American Automobile Manufacturers Association, the major lobbying group of Ford, General Motors Corp and Chrysler Corp, said the yen's fall "is becoming a serious problem which is disrupting U.S. business plannning and threatening many U.S. export opportunities."
The group said the issue requires the "immediate attention" of U.S. and Japanese government officials.
